I have farmed this land in Quzhou for fifty years. I am seventy-six now, and my legs are not as strong as they used to be, but I know every corner of my sixteen mu. My sons work in the city and send money home, so I can afford good inputs, but I still do the farming myself because this is what I know. The wheat I sowed last October is already in the ground—it is waking up now that the frost has passed. I will topdress it with urea at the jointing stage and run the well pump twice more before harvest: once now for the joints, and once when the grain is filling. I always give it four waters in a year, including the overwintering water I put down before the cold. I use an improved seed variety that my neighbor has also planted for years, and I rotary-till before sowing to break up the soil. I spray three times: herbicide in early spring, then fungicide and insecticide when the weather turns humid. For the summer maize, I never plough after wheat harvest—there is no time, and at my age I prefer the no-till seeder. I plant hybrid seed, the kind with the pink coating, because it gives me bigger ears. One bag of compound fertilizer goes down with the seed, and I spread urea at the big trumpet stage. The maize needs three waters, especially when it is tasseling. Two sprays: herbicide right after planting, and insecticide for borers later. I expect around 500 jin per mu of wheat and a bit more from the maize if the wind does not knock it down.
